provenance.notes:
OPTION SET IS CLOSED BY THE BINARY. `strings /usr/bin/sed | grep -E '^[A-Za-z:]{4,}$'` yields the getopt(3) string `EHI:ae:f:i:lnru`, which matches the man page option block exactly -- 11 options, four of them taking a value (I, e, f, i). Nothing is accepted that the page does not list, so `authoritative` is safe here. 

-i REQUIRES ITS EXTENSION OPERAND, AND THIS IS THE BIGGEST PORTABILITY TRAP IN THE TOOL. The getopt string spells it `i:`. `sed -i 's/a/X/' t1.txt` therefore consumes `s/a/X/` as the backup extension and then reads `t1.txt` as the SCRIPT: observed `sed: 2: "t1.txt": undefined label '1.txt'`, exit 1, file unmodified. The diagnostic depends on the first character of the filename -- the same command against `sedtest.txt` instead reports `unescaped newline inside substitute pattern`, because `s` opens a substitution where `t` opened a branch. Blast radius was checked and is smaller than it looks: `sed -i 's/a/X/' one.txt two.txt three.txt` exits 1 with `invalid command code o` and leaves all three files byte-identical. The failure is confusing, not destructive. `sed -i '' 's/a/X/' t2.txt` (empty extension, no backup) and `sed -i.bak 's/a/X/' t3.txt` (attached, writes t3.txt.bak) both succeed. The attached spelling is the one that also works on GNU, and is the only portable form.

-I AND -i ARE LAST-ONE-WINS, SO THEY ARE RECORDED AS conflicts_with. Both are accepted together (exit 0), so this is the silent-override case, not the diagnosed one. Probed with A.txt=`1\n2\n`, B.txt=`3\n4\n` and the script `$p`: `sed -I '' -i '' -n '$p' A.txt B.txt` leaves A=`2` B=`4` (per-file address space, -i won) while `sed -i '' -I '' -n '$p' A.txt B.txt` leaves A=empty B=`4` (one continuous address space, -I won). The result is decided by argument order alone, which a JSON object cannot express.

THE `w` FUNCTION WRITES FILES WITH NO -i ANYWHERE ON THE COMMAND LINE, AND TRUNCATES THEM BEFORE ANY INPUT IS READ. With w.out containing `PRECIOUS`, `sed 's/nomatch/x/w w.out' in.txt` exits 0 having matched nothing, and w.out is left empty. -a is the documented mitigation and it works: the same run as `sed -a 's/nomatch/x/w w.out' in.txt` leaves `PRECIOUS` intact. This is why the command is annotated destructive independently of -i/-I.

-E and -r are aliases (`-r  Same as -E for compatibility with GNU sed`), so they are NOT recorded as conflicting: `sed -E -r 's/a+/X/'` is accepted and produces the same result as either alone. -r is carried as its own entry because the format holds at most one short form per flag. Note -r appears in the first synopsis line's bundle `[-EHalnru]` but the man page SYNOPSIS in this release lists it in both forms; the getopt string settles that it is always accepted.

-l and -u are both accepted together (`sed -l -u` and `sed -u -l` both exit 0 with identical output) and no order-dependent difference could be observed, because sed emits whole lines either way. They are therefore NOT recorded as conflicting. Recorded as inconclusive rather than asserted in either direction.

END-OF-OPTIONS: `sed -- 's/a/X/' ./-weird.txt` is accepted (exit 0) and edits the dash-leading operand, so end_of_options is true. The separator only works in the option position: `sed 's/a/X/' -- ./-weird.txt` reports `sed: --: No such file or directory` and treats `--` as an input filename.

GRAMMAR: with no -e and no -f the first non-option operand is the script; with either present, every operand is an input file. Probed: `sed -e 's/a/X/' 's/a/Y/' g.txt` reports `sed: s/a/Y/: No such file or directory` and processes g.txt.

open_world IS SET FALSE AS A CHECKED NEGATIVE, not as a default. BSD sed has no GNU `e` flag: `printf 'x\n' | sed 's/x/echo PWNED/e'` is refused with `bad flag in substitute command: 'e'`, where the same script on GNU sed 4.9/4.10 executes and prints PWNED. The `w` function writes a file and cannot execute -- `sed -n 'w /dev/stdout'` just copies the line. So this variant reaches nothing beyond the filesystem, and the value records that it was checked rather than assumed.

description: Stream editor. Reads the specified files, or standard input if none are given, applies a list of editing commands to each line, and writes the result to standard output. A single command may be given as the first operand; multiple commands are given with -e or -f and are applied in the order specified regardless of origin. With -i or -I the files are edited in place instead, and the `w` function writes to named files whether or not in-place editing is on.

flags.description: Interpret regular expressions as extended (modern) regular expressions rather than basic regular expressions (BRE's). The re_format(7) manual page fully describes both formats.
Enable enhanced features in the regular expression syntax. This option is independent of the -E option.

Edit files in-place, saving backups with the specified extension. A zero-length extension saves no backup. In-place editing with -I takes place in a single continuous line address space covering all files: the line counter is never reset between files, address ranges can span file boundaries, and "$" matches only the last line of the last file.

Delay opening each file listed as a parameter to a "w" function until a command containing that function is applied to a line of input. By default those files are created (or truncated) before any processing begins.
Append the editing commands specified by the command argument to the list of commands.
Append the editing commands found in the file command_file to the list of commands. The commands should each be listed on a separate line, and are read from standard input if command_file is "-".

Edit files in-place similarly to -I, but treat each file independently: line numbers in each file start at 1, "$" matches the last line of the current file, and address ranges are limited to the current file. The extension operand is mandatory; give an empty string to save no backup.
Suppress the default behavior of echoing each line of input to standard output after all of the commands have been applied to it.
Same as -E, for compatibility with GNU sed.

positional_args.name: script
positional_args.description: A single editing command, taken from the first operand only when neither -e nor -f is given. If either is present this slot does not exist and every operand is an input file.

positional_args.name: file
positional_args.description: Input files. With none, standard input is read. With -i or -I these files are rewritten in place.
